extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of humor theory, cognitive/affective psychologists, philosophers of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic framework for explaining when and why situations or jokes are perceived as humorous, centering on competing affective interpretations (Violation vs Normality) and their relative strength. Designed for theorizing and evaluating humor phenomena in psychological and philosophical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective commitment to violated moral principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who do not laugh have greater affective commitments to the violated subjective moral principle than those who do; personal experience can increase affective involvement and reduce humor (example: a new mother finding a dead-baby joke no longer funny).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate perceiver's degree of emotional involvement or commitment to the principle being violated. High commitment -> offended/threatened responses; low commitment -> more likely to accept the violation as normal and laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous Violation (V) and Normality (N) interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: A funny violation occurs when a perceived violation is juxtaposed with a simultaneous view of the situation as normal (V AND N); humor requires copresence of the two views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether observers can construct both a Violation interpretation and a competing Normality interpretation of the same situation (possibly applied to different aspects). If both are present, the theory predicts humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-level scale of interpretation (not-V / V&N / V&not-N)
rubrics_metrics.description: Levels: Level 1 (not-V): lack of attachment -> no reaction; Level 2 (V and N): weak/detachable attachment -> humor; Level 3 (V and not-N): strong/non-detachable attachment -> offensiveness/threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify perceivers/situations into these three levels by measuring strength of affective commitment and presence/absence of N interpretation. Use this to predict whether humor, no reaction, or offense results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal distance and personal involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations often change over time from threatening (not funny) to funny as emotional involvement lessens; with long time/changed personal circumstances, situations may become unremarkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider temporal distance and whether the perceiver's emotional attachment to the particular instance has decreased. Greater temporal distance or reduced personal involvement increases likelihood of a normalizing interpretation and hence humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity/ambiguity of interpretations increases humor
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation may contain several violations and multiple possible N and V interpretations; uncovering multiple N and V elements can increase laughter — there need not be a single 'correct' interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating funniness, look for multiple independent V and N readings; more possible compatible interpretations tends to intensify humor (and different perceivers may latch on to different elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of humor: complexity, number, pleasure, familiarity, intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Among funny things, some are funnier because more of the elements (complexity, multiple violations, pleasurable N interpretations, familiarity, vividness/intensity of violation) are present or amplified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quantity and intensity of contributing elements: count distinct violations, degree of vividness or personal familiarity with the violation, and whether the N interpretation is gratifying (e.g., target disliked). Greater magnitude on these axes -> stronger perceived humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of presentation (N vs V sequencing not necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no necessary temporal ordering of N and V; humor requires copresence rather than a fixed order. Commonly N appears in setup and V in punchline, but V+N (V then reinterpretation as N) also produces humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat punchline order as an essential feature; evaluate whether copresence of N and V is achieved (by setup+punchline or by later reinterpretation). Both N->V and V->N orders can produce humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as emotional transformation (cause or consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be a consequence of reduced emotional pain (retrospection) or a cause of recategorizing painful situations as normal; it can thus liberate from V interpretations or, conversely, expose someone as the butt and cause negative transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether humor is being used to normalize and reduce pain (therapeutic/ameliorative) or whether laughter re-categorizes someone as responsible and thus harms them. Effects depend on whether mental recategorization is lasting and on contextual constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is not funny: offense vs absence of violation
rubrics_metrics.description: "That's not funny!" has two meanings: (1) offensive — the violated principle is held too dear and N interpretation cannot predominate; (2) "what's the point?" — there is no V Interpretation. Offense implies clear understanding of the point; lack of V implies perceiver not attached to relevant principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between absence of perceived violation and presence of a strong violation that provokes offense. Determine whether the perceiver 'gets it' (sees the violation) but rejects normalizing interpretation, or simply fails to see a violation at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social interpretation: laughter can be perceived as disrespect
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter communicates that the laugher finds a moral violation acceptable; if the laughed-at person (B) is emotionally committed to the violated principle (often personal dignity), they interpret A's laughter as viewing B's pain as acceptable and thus disrespectful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating social consequences, account for asymmetric affective commitments: shared humor may normalize and relieve, but unshared humor often produces feelings of disrespect in those attached to the violated principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity and incongruity must be the N-vs-V type
rubrics_metrics.description: While absurdity and incongruity are present in humor (because 'it's okay' and 'it's not okay' are incongruous), not all incongruity/absurdity is funny; the relevant kind is the absurdity of thinking a situation is simultaneously normal and a moral violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count generic incongruity as sufficient for humor. Evaluate whether the incongruity specifically juxtaposes normality and morally-significant violation (the N vs V kind).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal experience ('truth') amplifies humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that relate to things people have personally experienced are often judged 'so true' and can be especially funny because the perceiver recognizes the violation in their own life — seeing the violation in oneself doubles the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a joke maps onto the perceiver's personal experience; such mapping increases vividness of V interpretation and can amplify humor, though 'truth' is not essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggression and superiority are related consequences but insufficient explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggression-based and superiority-based theories capture some insights (e.g., humor can involve feeling superiority or latent aggression), but they are inadequate alone because humor can be non-aggressive and have ameliorative functions; superiority can arise when perceiver is not responsible for the violation while the butt is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining humor, consider aggression/superiority as possible consequences or contributing aspects, but not as sole theoretical bases. Check whether copresence of V and N better accounts for the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive predicate structure of N and V (N(p), V(q))
rubrics_metrics.description: N and V are interpretive predicates that apply to propositions/aspects of a complex situation (e.g., N(p) and V(q)); they need not be logically inconsistent when applied to different propositions, which allows affective absurdity to be possible in complex situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze which aspects/propositions of a situation each predicate applies to; use predicate-like notation (N(p), V(q)) to clarify that apparent contradiction can arise from different argument structure and scope rather than logical impossibility.
